title: Rooftop HVAC Service: Guard the Skylights
summary: An HVAC technician working on rooftop units tripped on the lip of an unguarded skylight and fell about 26 feet to a concrete floor. No fall protection was in use. Find and guard skylights before any rooftop work starts.
talking_points: In this incident, three workers had been changing belts on rooftop units for about four hours. The roof was flat and the skylights were unguarded. The technician turned to talk to a coworker, tripped on a skylight lip, and fell through.
Skylights usually cannot hold a person's weight. Treat every skylight as a hole.
Before work starts, assess the roof for fall hazards. Do this for maintenance work, not only for new construction.
Protect skylights with a guardrail system, a cover or screen, or a personal fall arrest system (body harness, lanyard, connectors, and anchor points).
Covers must be strong enough for the weight placed on them, secured against moving, and marked HOLE or COVER.
Stay aware of where skylights are when you walk, turn, or talk. Do not walk backward or look away while moving.
Wear fall protection when skylights are not guarded. PPE should be used after other reasonable ways to reduce the hazard have been tried.
Building owners, designers, and contractors should consider guarding skylights with screens or guardrails for workers who must work on the roof.
site_hazards_to_check: Unguarded skylights or skylights with low curbs that you can trip on
Skylights, hatches, and roof openings along the path to the rooftop units
No guardrails, screens, or covers on skylights
No anchor points or harnesses for the crew
Workers walking and talking, carrying parts, or turning near skylights
discussion_questions: Where are all the skylights and roof openings on this roof, and how are they guarded?
What fall protection will each of us use on this roof?
What could distract you while you move around the roof, and how do we manage that?
